title: Cool ways to use solar panels on campus
summary: In this issue of our environmental newsletter, we get a university campus tour featuring some neat ways to use solar panels; see what's happening to old EV batteries instead of recycling; and find…

blocks.text: Welcome to our weekly newsletter where we highlight environmental trends and solutions that are moving us to a more sustainable world.

blocks.text: Cool ways to use solar panels on campus

Joshua Pearce gives his students a tour of the solar panels on top of the Amit Chakma Engineering Building at Western University in London, Ont. (Free Appropriate Sustainability Technology (FAST) Lab at Western University)
A lot has changed since Joshua Pearce started in solar energy research more than 25 years ago.

“When I was a PhD student, you’d go to an energy conference and they’d almost laugh at you as a solar guy — like go back to your Lego blocks, we’re going to do ‘real energy’ with fossil fuels,” he said.
“Now, it’s the other way around, coal plants cannot compete with solar.”
Through technological advancements and the increased adoption of solar technologies, it is becoming much cheaper and easier to install solar panels, and create creative designs with them.
Pearce is now the Chair of Innovation at Western University in London, Ont., and solar is a booming industry in many parts of the world, though not necessarily in Canada.

And it’s not just huge solar arrays in fields. Pearce gave a photo tour of some of the interesting solar-powered installations at his university, from a picnic table to a mural. While they're only for demonstration and not commercially available, it's an interesting view of what's possible.
A picnic table with a plug
One of Pearce’s graduate students' first projects, a picnic table that can charge electronic devices. (FAST Lab at Western University)
This solar-powered picnic table is one of Pearce’s favourite applications.
It is made from recycled materials, including decommissioned panels from a solar farm and recycled plastic lumber, and creates enough power to charge laptops and cell phones.
The table sits in the engineering garden at Western University.
Cool designs now possible
One of Pearce’s students stands in front of a mural made of solar panels at Western University. (FAST Lab at Western University)
This angel wing mural is actually made up of solar panels.
“If you give up 10 to 20 per cent efficiency, you can make your solar panel look like whatever you want,” said Pearce.
“It can look like trees, the sky, bricks, your favourite cartoon character, dragons — whatever you want.”
That makes it possible to integrate solar panels as cladding, balcony railings, or coloured glass on windows — a growing trend called building-integrated photovoltaics (BIPV).
Solar panels can come in a variety of colours now. (FAST Lab at Western University)
Solar panels can help increase agriculture yield
Solar panels can be installed either between rows of crops, or above crops that don’t need full sun exposure.

Pearce says that farmers can get more food out of the crops this way, compared to an open field, because the panels provide shade for crops that don’t need direct sunlight, or shelter from things like wind and hail.
He’s done experiments in Ontario which showed that, with solar panels set up, farms can get 18 per cent more strawberries, and almost double the number of pumpkins compared to normal farms.
Plus, sheep can graze under panels that provide shade, reducing the need to mow.
Other examples
Koami Hayibo, one of Pearce’s students, researches floating photovoltaic systems and their benefits. These solar panels are enough to power a house. (Submitted by Koami Soulemane Hayibo)
Other examples include solar fences, which Pearce says can be cheaper than wood fences in some instances, and can power things like pool water pumps.
Floating solar panels on water can also be beneficial because the water cools the panels, and the panels stop water from evaporating.
“We've looked at doing this in lakes that are going to die out if you don't conserve the water in some way, and that's a really great way to do it,” said Pearce.
He suggests that part of the lakes could be covered with floating panels, which can be done without disrupting fishing and swimming.
Pearce is excited about the future of solar energy — to help the environment, but also because in many cases, he says it’s becoming more cost-effective than using other building materials.
— Bridget Stringer-Holden

Reader feedback
Last week, Bridget Stringer-Holden wrote about efforts to bring back the mottled duskywing and two other rare species of butterfly.

That prompted Allan Baker of Toronto to share a photo with us and University of Guelph researcher Ryan Norris. He wrote: "I spotted a species called the wild indigo duskywing on a marigold plant in our garden here in Toronto (Guildwood Village) on Aug. 1, 2026. Not knowing the species of this beautiful butterfly, I consulted iNaturalist to identify it. May this be of some help to your research."
In his reply, Norris wrote that this more common species is not endangered or threatened.
"But thanks for keeping an eye out,” wrote the ecologist. “Fun fact: this is the species we practice on for captive rearing before we did the real thing with mottled duskywing. Good identification."

The Big Picture: A new job for old EV batteries
(Nick Nesbitt/Mapleview Energy)

The batteries in this photo once worked in a mine. They powered a special kind of EV — electric underground mining vehicles made by MacLean Engineering. But now they have a new job working at a farm in Elora, Ont.

The woman in the photo is Sandra Aragon Aviles, battery systems engineer at Mapleview Energy. The Ontario startup launched a pilot this summer that repurposed batteries from about four mining vehicles into a battery-and-solar system that has so far cut the farm's power costs by 37 per cent.

I met the company's founder and CEO Nick Nesbitt last week at the MaRS Climate Impact conference in Toronto. The timing was perfect, as I had been writing about what happens to EV batteries when they're no longer suitable for powering vehicles. Many EV battery recyclers have gone bankrupt. But more and more EV batteries are being repurposed as energy storage batteries at places like farms, factories and airports to save energy costs and provide emergency backup power. You can read more about this trend here.
— Emily Chung

items: Melting glaciers are expanding glacial lakes. This has well-known downsides, such as a risk of dangerous outburst floods. But there is a way to reduce that risk while generating large amounts of renewable power, scientists have found.

Launched in 2020, Project Arrow aimed to build the first Canadian-made zero-emission concept vehicle, from critical minerals to manufacturing to automotive software. Corporate Knights checks where it's at now.

In the 1990s, 80,000 cars a day drove through the small city of Pontevedra, Spain, with a population of just 85,000. Then in 1999, the residents decided to get rid of cars. Reasons to Be Cheerful looks at how that went.
Despite evolving for millennia to thrive in the blazing Sonoran Desert, the iconic saguaro cactus is struggling to survive escalating heat waves.
First came "Super El Niño." Then "Godzilla El Niño." Now there's a new monster in town: "Mega El Niño." At this rate, King Ghidorah may be next. But has this year's El Niño really been upgraded?

blocks.text: B.C. First Nation aims to be model for wildfire prevention
Lori Daniels with the UBC Centre for Wildfire Coexistence, left, and Chief George Lampreau of the Simpcw First Nation in an area of forest being remedied. (Dave Dormer/CBC)
A First Nation in the B.C. Interior is hoping to be the model for wildfire resilience across the province.

The Simpcw First Nation, whose reserve is near Barriere, has partnered with the University of British Columbia's Centre for Wildfire Coexistence and the Co-Operators Resilience Acceleration Lab to form the Simpcw Wildfire Resilience Coalition.
The goal is to reduce the risk of wildfire around the community about 75 kilometres north of Kamloops.
The project involves a 1.5-square-kilometre cutblock, where crews have spent the last two years studying the land, then using heavy machinery to thin out trees and remove underbrush.
Around two-thirds of the trees and brush will be removed.
An area of forest prior to having trees and underbrush removed as part of the Simpcw Wildfire Resilience Coalition project. (Dave Dormer/CBC)
"If you look up the hills, you can see how thick the mountainside is, that's what we're reducing," said Simpcw Chief George Lampreau.
"Because if [a wildfire] gets into that, it'll spread across the top, and we're hopeful if it'll hit this, there's not enough trees to keep it going."
Lampreau added that planting trees is also part of wildfire mitigation.
"Instead of just coming back and planting some pine that'll grow fast, we're going to look at planting more of the birch, the aspen, so those ones will help contain the fires," he said.
The trees are processed and sold after removal in an effort to recoup some of the cost.
Lori Daniels, a co-director of UBC's Centre for Wildfire Coexistence, said that a goal of the project is to leave larger Douglas fir trees, which provide shade and are used by birds and animals.
Don Iveson is an executive adviser with Co-operators Resilience Accelleration Lab and says planning and paperwork for these types of projects can take years.
"One of the things we are working through with this project, is to understand where are the places where that permitting process can be more streamlined," he said.

"What advice can we give to the government of B.C. about making it easier for treatments like this to move ahead economically — so they can produce jobs, produce fibre supply, but also achieve risk-reduction in a timely fashion?"
If the project proves to be successful, Lampreau says he'd like to see the partnership model be used by other First Nations and communities around the province.
— Dave Dormer
